analysis.one_liner: Caps jury awards for pain and suffering in pregnancy and emergency-care malpractice lawsuits at $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have capped pain-and-suffering awards in obstetric and emergency-care malpractice cases at $250,000, never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee with just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for malpractice lawsuits involving pregnancy care, obstetrics, gynecology, and emergency or trauma care. It would cap compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, make punitive damages very hard to win, reduce awards by insurance benefits the patient already received, cap lawyers' fees on a sliding scale, and prevent doctors from being sued for prescribing an FDA-approved drug. It would also override state laws that give patients more generous remedies in these cases.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries would be medical malpractice insurers and the doctors, hospitals, and drug makers facing lawsuits over obstetric, gynecological, and emergency care, because the bill limits how much they can be made to pay. Injured patients with strong documented financial losses (medical bills, lost wages) would keep full recovery of those economic damages, and the bill would cap lawyers' contingency fees so a larger share of any award reaches the claimant. Supporters' stated purpose was to lower liability costs enough to keep obstetricians and emergency rooms serving patients.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would leave economic damages — medical bills, lost earnings, and other verifiable financial losses — entirely uncapped, so a catastrophically injured patient's measurable costs would still be fully recoverable.

It would cap lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% of anything above $600,000) and let courts police fee arrangements, with the stated aim of sending more of any award to the injured patient rather than the attorney.
It would apply a fair-share rule so each defendant pays only its own percentage of responsibility instead of being jointly liable for the full judgment.

Supporters' stated premise, in the bill's own title, was that the liability system placed an excessive burden on delivering obstetric and emergency care and that these limits would improve patients' access to those services.

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously injured by malpractice during pregnancy, emergency, or trauma care would bear the cost, because the $250,000 cap applies to pain-and-suffering damages — often the largest part of an award for someone left disabled. Punitive damages would require near-criminal-level proof, awards would be reduced by insurance the patient already had, and state laws giving patients stronger remedies would be overridden in these cases. Plaintiffs' attorneys would also lose fee income under the mandated sliding-scale caps.

drawbacks.text: A flat $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages falls hardest on patients whose injuries are devastating but whose financial losses are small — children, stay-at-home parents, and retirees — because their compensation for a lifetime of disability would be limited even when a provider was clearly negligent.

Punitive damages would be available only on clear and convincing evidence of malicious intent to injure or deliberate failure to avoid certain injury — a standard ordinary malpractice almost never meets — and could not even be requested in the initial complaint.

Awards would be reduced by any health, disability, or workers' compensation benefits the patient was entitled to, letting the party that caused the injury benefit from insurance the patient (or taxpayers) already paid for.

The bill would preempt state law: states with stronger patient protections, longer filing deadlines, or higher damages would be overridden in these cases, shifting rulemaking from state courts and legislatures to a single federal standard.
A provider who prescribed an FDA-approved drug or device could not be named in a product-liability suit, cutting off a pathway to recovery for patients harmed by a medication used in their care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuinely patient-friendly pieces — uncapped economic damages, fee caps, and the fair-share rule — are outweighed by its central design: a flat $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages and a near-prohibition on punitive damages that would most reduce compensation precisely in the worst childbirth and emergency-care injuries. The claim that these limits would improve access to obstetric and emergency care was the bill's stated rationale, but it died without a hearing, so it was never tested or debated on the merits. An honest supporter would also have to defend overriding state laws that chose to give patients stronger remedies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2005, and referred the same day to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
It had only one cosponsor and never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the committee.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with the bill still stalled in committee, so its caps on malpractice awards never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained, because the bill changed nothing: injured patients kept whatever remedies their state law allowed, and malpractice insurers and providers continued operating under the existing rules. The bill's quiet death also meant its supporters' caps were never tested or enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; it died quietly in committee

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as its Senate sponsor.

for.name: Sen. John Ensign
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: American Medical Association
for.what_they_did: Led the national campaign for federal medical malpractice damage caps during this period, the policy this bill embodied.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, which sat with it until the Congress ended.

against.name: American Association for Justice (trial lawyers)
against.what_they_did: Fought federal malpractice damage caps throughout this era as a threat to injured patients' compensation.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred, so no party split can be measured; the bill's only supporters of record were its two Republican Senate sponsors.

industries.note: Caps on noneconomic and punitive damages, and the collateral-source reduction, directly cut the amounts insurers must pay on malpractice claims involving obstetric and emergency care. The bill's central effect is to lower their payouts.

industries.industry: Physicians and hospitals providing obstetric, gynecological, and emergency care
industries.note: The bill would sharply limit their liability exposure in obstetric and emergency cases, including shielding providers from product-liability suits over FDA-approved drugs they prescribe. Providers argued this would keep doctors practicing and emergency rooms open; the cost falls on patients who are injured and undercompensated.

The bill caps contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% above $600,000) and lets courts redirect fees, cutting deeply into the contingency-fee business model for malpractice cases.

Doctors who prescribe FDA-approved drugs and devices could not be named in product-liability or class-action suits, removing a common route by which injured patients reach the manufacturers and sellers behind those products.

Awards would be reduced by health and disability benefits the patient already received, shifting more injury costs onto health coverage, though insurers retain subrogation rights to recover those payments.
